elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: New § 11.3: "Corio, as the customer, may terminate this Agreement for convenience upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One." The element is disjunctive; an Agreement-level right suffices, and the document contains no Order Form structure, so no Order Form/partial-termination language is required.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: § 11.3 sets the trigger at "thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One" — exactly the 30-day ceiling, in writing, given by Corio.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: § 11.3: "Commerce One shall refund to Corio, pro rata, any prepaid fees for the period after the effective date of termination." The words "pro rata" are express, not merely inferred from a post-termination refund period, and the refund is expressly tied to the convenience termination.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: § 11.3: "Commerce One shall have no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the initial five (5) year term or any renewal term." Retained § 11.1 lets either party give notice "at least thirty (30) days prior to the expiration of the initial five (5) year term or any one (1) year renewal thereof of its intention to terminate" — that notice takes effect at expiration, so it is natural-term non-renewal evaluated under RENEWAL, not a mid-term Vendor convenience exit; § 11.2 is breach/insolvency only.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: § 11.3 fixes notice at thirty (30) days, which is the preferred figure and falls outside the 60–90 day fallback band. Not a defect, since the proposal targets the preferred level.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: neither the original §§ 11.1–11.2 nor new § 11.3 imposes any early-termination fee, penalty, or accelerated payment on Corio's exit, so there is no fee to cap.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: § 11.3 bars any Commerce One convenience termination "during the initial five (5) year term or any renewal term," leaving only the § 11.1 non-renewal notice whose effect is tied to expiration of the then-current term.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: The only Vendor-side exit notice left is § 11.1's "at least thirty (30) days prior to the expiration" non-renewal notice; nothing in the redline raises Vendor notice to 90 days. Immaterial here because the preferred checklist is complete.

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: all four preferred elements (Customer convenience right, ≤30 days' written notice, express pro-rata refund of prepaid fees, no Vendor convenience right during the committed term) appear in operative § 11.3, not merely in the margin comment.

The deterministic check "Customer convenience termination present: false" is a pattern-matching artefact, not a substantive gap: the interposed apposition "Corio, as the customer, may terminate this Agreement for convenience" breaks a contiguous actor-verb match while stating the right in full operative terms. Inspected in substance, the right is present.

Finding kind is correctly a deviation (missing behaviour): the five-year term with automatic one-year renewals offers exits only for uncured material breach or insolvency, so the document failed both preferred and fallback before the edit.

Minimal: one concise inserted section numbered into the existing Section 11 scheme; §§ 11.1 and 11.2 are retained verbatim (including their original typography), no survival tail, no at-own-expense or procedural boilerplate, no added damages or notice mechanics, and no words removed from outside the target elements. Correctly omits "in whole or in part" from the model language, since there is no Order Form or partial-termination structure to support it.

Preserves intent: the breach and insolvency exits, the renewal cadence, and the § 11.1 non-renewal notice all survive without contradiction; § 11.3's bar operates on mid-term convenience exits while § 11.1's notice operates at expiration, so no retained sentence is negated and no cross-reference or defined term is left dangling.

Fallback level is not independently complete (30-day rather than 60–90-day Customer notice; no 90-day Vendor notice), which is expected and acceptable — the comment offers the fallback as a negotiation step rather than implementing it.
